What are neurons? What do they do?
{{ Neurons }} are brain cells that send and receive signals. By connecting with other neurons, they allow information to travel through the brain. Your brain has about 86 billion neurons!
Tiny gaps between connected neurons are called {{ synapses }}. Chemical signals travel across synapses, carrying messages from one neuron to the next.
What is the brain? How does it work?
The {{ brain }} controls thinking, memory, movement, and the senses. It is also where our memories are formed and stored.
Inside the brain, a massive network of cells processes information. These cells are called {{ neurons }}, and memory depends on how they connect to each other.
What does the brain look like on a microscopic scale?
Scientists study brain connections at a {{ microscopic scale. }} They scan thousands of thin brain slices. These slices are 3,000x thinner than a human hair!
What can scientists see in those images?
The images are detailed enough to show tiny structures in the brain, including neurons and blood vessels.
What has Professor Axon been working on? What's his story?

Professor Axon is a {{ neuroscientist }} who has dedicated his life to studying the brain. His goal has always been to create a {{ 3D map }} of brain connections related to memory. He has worked on it for decades - and still isn’t close to finishing!
What is he doing in Polar Peaks?

Professor Axon moved to Polar Peaks to investigate the locals’ forgetfulness. He believes that mapping brain {{ connections }} involved in memory could help reveal what is going wrong. But the work is very slow to do by hand. He needs your help to train an {{ AI model }} to speed up the research.
How do scientists manually map the brain's connections?

Mapping brain connections by hand is an incredibly slow process. Scientists must manually examine scans of tiny brain slices to identify and {{ label }} neurons, the brain cells that send and receive signals.
How does labeling help scientists map the brain?
After labeling the cells in each scan, scientists stack the scans together. This builds a 3D map that shows how the neurons connect to each other.
Experiential AI literacy for every classroom

AI Quests is a game-based learning experience designed to teach middle school students (ages 11-14) about AI. Through a series of interactive, code-free quests, students will learn what it takes to responsibly build AI applications that address real-world societal challenges. The quests are inspired by actual AI projects led by Google Research.

Developed by Google Research and the Stanford Accelerator for Learning, AI Quests is designed to promote active learning. It empowers students to explore, analyze, and reflect on their own understanding as they complete each quest. This makes AI Quests a perfect complementary resource for existing in-class AI literacy programs, giving educators the flexibility to use it in whatever way supports their learning goals.
Committed to closing the literacy gap

Equipping K-12 students with AI literacy is essential for their future participation in an AI-driven world, preparing them as informed citizens, critical consumers, and potential future developers. At Google Research, we're not just developing AI tools and technologies; we're also committed to teaching students how to use AI responsibly in the world and workplace of tomorrow.
AI Quests is free and open to all.
AI Quests is an open and self-service resource for you to use right away. If you'd like to explore a deeper partnership or collaboration, please contact us at
What age group is AI Quests suitable for?

We designed the quests for middle school students (ages 11-14), however educators are more than welcome to adapt the lesson plan to accommodate other age groups. We have received feedback from users who have even adapted this experience to educate adults!
Where and by whom is AI Quests intended to be delivered?
AI Quests is an in-class resource designed to compliment existing AI literacy programs, such as
. It also includes comprehensive teacher guides, providing all the guidance needed to run it independently in subject classes as well (e.g. Geography or Science).
Do students need to know how to code in order to play AI Quests?
No code is required, this is a no-code gaming experience.
Will AI Quests be available in other languages?
Multiple languages are available and can be accessed in the drop down menu in the footer. More languages are being added so please check back here for updates.

Do I need an internet connection for AI Quests?
Yes, AI Quests is a web-based game, so you will need an internet connection to play AI Quests.
Does AI Quests use Google’s AI capabilities?

AI Quests focuses on showing teens how humans can initiate and design AI applications that can address some of humanity's biggest unsolved challenges. In order to maximize access to this game and to make it adaptable for all curricula, there is no use of Generative AI experiences within the game itself.
What information do you collect on the users of AI Quests?

We do not collect any personally identifiable information through AI Quests. We do not require users to input their name, login, email, or any other piece of data in order to play AI Quests. To continuously improve the experience, we collect anonymous aggregated gameplay metrics including average length of time it takes users to complete each quest and other performance metrics.
What are some of the key pedagogical principles at the heart of AI Quests?

Across quests, activities build cumulative understanding of the AI development cycle and its societal impact. Guided by Stanford Accelerator for Learning, the core pedagogy in AI Quests is built on three core pillars: Situated Learning, Authentic Practice that mirrors real AI and data work, and Game-Based Learning to maximize student motivation to learn.

Google Research is the division of Google dedicated to fundamental and applied research in computer science and related fields. Its primary mission is to advance the state-of-the-art in technology, often tackling long-term, large-scale challenges.
What is the Stanford Accelerator for Learning and what is their role in AI Quests?

The Stanford Accelerator for Learning is an interdisciplinary research initiative at Stanford's Graduate School of Education dedicated to creating and scaling effective, equitable learning solutions. For AI Quests, they serve as the primary co-creator alongside Google Research, providing the core pedagogical expertise to design the game's structure, story-based challenges, and active learning components.

Every family has stories worth saving. Grandpa had 200 in Tamil, buried in WhatsApp, so twin 7th graders built WisTree, an app that uses AI to translate voice notes into English. (Technovation)
Youth winner Ahana Chatterjee from the United States coded Food Flow, helping users make smarter, healthier choices while improving food access. (MIT App Inventor)
Project: ALBATROSS is a bio-inspired autopilot that teaches a small RC glider to “ride” the wind like an albatross and stretch every watt of battery power. (Raspberry Pi Foundation)
Farming can be a risky business, unless you have the right tools. Using the KisanSaathi app, farmers scan crop leaves, classify plant health, and receive personalized advice. (MIT App Inventor)
Akshay developed a machine learning model to detect microburst damage using image analysis. Deployed on a Raspberry Pi with a camera, the system achieved 100% success. (Raspberry Pi Foundation)
Kids with long illnesses often cannot go to school. Star Connect is a safe space to share feelings with friends, and AI spots when someone is struggling so a parent can help. (Technovation)
An app created to swap screen time for offline adventures. Gemini AI personalizes activities by age and interest, mapped to Madrid's public libraries, parks and sports facilities. (Technovation)
Kinesign translates sign language into text and speech. A youth team from Uruguay built the app using Teachable Machine and TensorFlow to reduce communication barriers. (MIT App Inventor)

Insight Reader is an automated book-flipping device that captures images of each page and uses AI to analyse the content, making physical books more interactive and accessible. (Raspberry Pi Foundation)
AI has some unusual uses! The image-classifier app, EcoBin, rewards households, street vendors, and restaurants that recycle used cooking oil instead of dumping it down the drain. (MIT App Inventor)

TideGuard AI is an open-source platform that forecasts where and when floating plastic will accumulate on the coast, so volunteers can clean it up before it breaks into microplastics (Raspberry Pi Foundation)
This AI-powered phone app, called Hearo, helps children with hearing impairments improve their speech and listening skills. (MIT App Inventor)
Learning science in a new language is hard when you are six. Point this app at a textbook picture and AI names it in English and says it out loud, so you can practice alone. (Technovation)
Birds show if a wetland is healthy, and wetlands are home to 40% of all species. Fewer people are left to count them, so AI counts the birds and a game gets kids watching too. (Technovation)
EcoMonitor is an AI-driven plant health monitoring system using moisture sensors and cameras to help users maintain plant health via real-time app notifications. (Raspberry Pi Foundation)
Many older people in Nigeria live alone after family moves away. AgeWell is a phone app with an AI chat helper that reminds them to take medicine and calls for help if they fall. (Technovation)
Uzbek Sign Language users cannot always be understood. Remu uses a camera and AI to turn their signs into spoken Uzbek, and Remu Academy teaches signing through short games. (Technovation)
